caseno: F.M.A.T. No. 21 of 1975 with C.R. No. 20 (fm)/75 and Civil Revision No. 1365 of 1974.
lawyer:
M.H. Khandker, Md. Shafiqur Rahman------ For the appellant. 
Moinul Hossain, Mozammel Haque Khan, Joinul Abedin------ For Respondent No. 1.
 S.R. Paul, R.K. Bhattacharya, Md. Shah Alam------ For added respondents.
parties:
Khwaja Nur Mohammad and others ------ Appellant,
Vs.
Khwaja Abdul Gani and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.—These two matters viz. F.M.A.T. No. 21 of 1975 and Civil Rule No. 1365 of 1974 have been heard analogously. The Civil Rule is directed against on order dated 11-12-74 passed by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca in Title Execution Case No. 39 of 1963 rejecting an application for staying the works of a Receiver and the appeal is directed against an order passed in the said Title Execution case on the 1st January, 1975 rejecting an application for cancellation of the appointment of the Receiver. 

 2. The facts leading to the passing of the aforesaid impugned orders, which are spread over a period of about 18 years, may be briefly stated as follows: Mosammat Sara Kulsum Begum and others instituted a suit with the permission of the Court under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure being Title Suit No. 130 of 1957 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for a declaration that certain properties as described in the schedules to the plaint as well as the compensation money amounting to Tk. 1,8,3,751.65 were Wakf properties that the maintenance and other allowances payable to the beneficiaries including the Plaintiffs under the Wakf as well as an agreement of 1881 were charged upon the properties in the suit. There was also a prayer for temporary injunction in the said suit for directing the Mutwalli to invest the aforesaid compensation money or any other money which might be made available by conversion of any part of the Wakf properties in purchasing some other properties or in some other profitable transaction under the supervision and control of the court in the interest of the beneficiaries as well as the Wakf. 

 3. The suit was contesting by the defendants represented by the Manager of the Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards, by filing a written statement in which strong objections were taken to the prayers made in the plaint. The suit was ultimately decreed on the 3rd September, 1959 in terms of a petition of compromise filed on behalf of both the parties. The terms of the Said compromise decree which are relevant for our present purpose may be quoted as follows: 

 "(1) The Court of Wards on behalf of the defendants shall pay a total sum of rupees 10 lakhs to a Board of Trustees consisting of 11 (eleven) persons named below and constituted by a Deed of Trust executed by the plaintiffs on their behalf and on behalf of the persons represented by them and to be registered hereinafter. The names of the members of the first Board of Trustees are: 

 (a) That as soon as the Dilkusha properties are sold, transferred or acquitted by the Govt. the Court of Wards "shall pay to the aforesaid Board of Trustees a sum of rupees one Lakh in cash and, in lieu of a sum of rupees four lakhs, shall transfer to the said Board of Trustees by a registered deed, free from all encumbrances, and give vacant possession of the properties described in the Schedule 'A' below to the said of Trustees, and the Board of Trustees shall accept the properties described in the Schedule 'A' in lieu of the sum of rupees four lakhs. 

 (b) That simultaneously or thereafter within five years from hence, the Court of Wards shall dispose of the Ahsan Manzil properties as described in schedule `B' below and shall pay out of the sale proceeds a sum of rupees Five lakhs forth-with to the said Board of Trustees, to holds it for the benefit of the Plaintiffs and the persons represented by them, according to the terms and conditions as laid down in the said Deed of Trust. 

 Provided, however, that in case of the Ahsan Manzil properties as described in schedule 'B' below being disposed of or sold piecemeal, the Court of Wards undertakes to pay not less than 33 percent sale proceeds of each deal to cover the five lakhs within five years to the Board of Trustees. 

 4. The undertakings relating to payment of money and transfer of the properties as had been given, in the aforesaid compromise decree having not been fulfilled, at first Title Execution Case No. 22 of 1961 was started and the same was disposed of without any effect. Thereafter the present Title Execution case No. 39 of 1963 as initiated on 25-11-63 and the same is suit pending till today. Certain steps were taken at first to realize the decretal money amounting to Rs. 6,00,000/- by attaching certain properties under Order 21 rules 43 and 46 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The execution proceeding was contested by the judgment-debtors at certain stages. On 29-8-64, on the pray or of the Decree-holders for enforcing transfer of Schedule 'A' property, as provided in the compromise decree, the Executing Court directed a draft copy of the proposed Kabala to be served upon the judgment debtors under Order 21 Rule 43 C.P.C. and also issued notice upon the Manager, Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate asking him to produce Income Tax Clearance Certificate in Court by 20-9-64 or in default to write a letter to Income Tax Authority to have their dues paid out of the money in deposit and issue the necessary certificates. Thereafter on 1-6-65 the Decree holders applied for realization of Rs. 6,00,000/-by attachment and sale of Ahsan Manzil properties belonging to the Judgment-debtors and ultimately sale proclamation was issued under Order 21 Rule 66 CPC fixing a date of Sale of the attached properties. After this on 16-6-66 judgment debtors deposited the entire detrital dues with cost amounting to Tk. 6,00, 000'25 paisa in Court. Meanwhile, the decree holders continued to pursue their remedy for enforcing the transfer of the property as provided in the petition of compromise. 

 "(4) that so far as the question of fulfillment of the remaining terms of clause 1(a) ,the judgment debtors have stated repeatedly that they are always ready and willing to perform their part of the agreement. The Board of Revenue was pleased to request the judgment-debtors to obtain their respective Clearance Certificates but only a few of them have succeeded to contain the same and most of them have failed to obtain the same. The judgment debtors are 115 co-sharers residing in Pakistan, U.K., U.S.A. and other parts of the world and to obtain all their income Tax Clearance Certificates at a time and within a stipulated period is really a difficult job. It will be evident from paragraph 7 of the decree holder's petn also that the Clearance Certificate are not being spent even though the same were written for from this learned Court as early as on 16-6-65. It is evident and admitted that the documents cannot be registered without the said Clearance Certificates. So far these judgment debtors are concerned they are always ready and willing to execute the necessary deeds. These Judgment-debtors duly approved the draft deed also with necessary modification as embodied in their written objection filed in Court earlier. 

 (5) That in spite of the best efforts of these judgment debtors and the direction of this Court to the Income Tax Authority the transfer of the properties could not yet be made for reasons beyond the control of these judgment debtors to liquidate their date of the aforesaid balance sum of Rs. 4,00,000/- (Four lacs) out of the total sum of Rs. 11,00,000/- (Eleven lacs). 

 6. As it appears from the order dated 31-1-69, the prayer made in the aforesaid petition did not find favour with the executing court which held that it was a matter for amicable adjustment between the parties but the executing Court permitted the Decree holder to pay the Income Tax dues of the judgment debtors, which would be the bring Income Tax Clearance" Certificate by 10-3-69. It was submitted on behalf of the decree-holders to the Court that no certificate of Income Tax Clearance was available in order to effect the transfer according to the decree, as the judgment debtors had not made payment of the Income Tax, dues. On 7-11-70 an application appears to have been filed on behalf of the decree holders in which it was stated that as directed by the order dated 31-1-69, the decree holders were trying to obtain the income Tax Clearance Certificate but as the matter might take some time as there were numerous judgment debtors, the decree holders were being deprived of the profits of the properties decreed in their favour for a number of years and a prayer was made in that application for directing the judgment debtors represented by the Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards to give immediate possession of the properties described in schedule A and E and also to execute and register the deed of transfer after obtaining the Income Tax Clearance Certificate. Another application to the similar effect was again filed on behalf of the decree holders on 15-12-70. 

 7. Nothing of any consequence seems to have happened in the said Execution Case during the years 1971-72. The case records also appear to have not been submitted to the Court for a sufficiently long period on the alleged ground of oversight more than once. If appears that on 11-5-73 the decree holders appeared by filing a fresh Vokalatnama and submitted an application with a prayer for directing the judgment debtors represented by the Chief Manager, Dacca Nawab Court of Wards to give immediate possession of Schedule A and E properties to the Trustees representing the decree holders and also for a direction upon the judgment debtors to execute and register the deed of transfer in terms of the decree lifter obtaining the Income Tax Clearance Certificate. This application was rejected by the Executing Court by its order dated 20-7-73 on the ground that the prayer for delivery of possession was premature. It was however, observed in the said order that the decree holders might apply for appointment of a Receiver if they so liked. 

 8. Thereafter on 31-7-73 the decree holder filed an application under section 51(d) read with Order 40 rule 1 C.P. Code for appointment of a Receiver of the Schedule A and E properties of the compromise decree and to commit the said properties to the custody and management of the Receiver, and to confer upon the Receiver all such powers for the realization, management, protection, preservation, maintenance and improvement of the said properties, the collection of the rent and profits thereof and disposal of the same in accordance with the direction of the Court. On that date the judgment debtors were granted time for filing written objection, if any, in the matter, but they did not, however, file any objection thereafter nor did they take any further steps in the matter. On 3-9-73 the executing Court by its order appointed Respondent No. 1 who has been described as one of the executors and trustees of Maulvi Khawaja Abdullah Welfare Trust as Receiver of the Schedule A and E properties and the Receiver furnished the necessary surety bond on 7-9-73. 

 9. It appears that the Receiver had taken various steps after his appointment for bringing the properties in question under his possession. On 18-4-74 he filed a petition for approval of the Court for demolition of the existing Kotwali building at 15 Wise Ghat Road, Dhaka which was said to be old and for, disposal of the materials of the demolished structures. On 24-4e74 he filed a copy of the resolution of the Trustees regarding demolition of the said building. The Executing Court by its order dated 29-4-74 appointed the Sheristadar of the Court to inspect and submit a report as to the condition of the building by making a local inspection. The Sheristadar submitted the report on 10-5-74 and the Executing Court allowed the prayer of the Receiver to demolish the building which according to the report of the Sheristadar, was dilapidated and old and required to be demolished. It appears that in pursuance of the said order the Receiver took possession of the said building and pulled it down in terms of the order of the Court. On 4-7-74 the decree holders filed a petition with a prayer to direct the Receiver to undertake the construction of a commercial market at 15 Wise Ghat Road, Dhaka immediately and submit a plan of the proposed construction. On 15-7-74 the Receiver filed a plan and an estimate of the cost of the proposed construction, whereupon the Court directed the Chief Engineer, C & B, Building Division, Dhaka to assist the Court in verifying the plan and the estimates of costs, as regards the genuineness and feasibility of the same. In the order dated 30-9-74 it is stated that the map of the proposed construction has been approved by the D.I.T. and the estimates of the same were found to be genuine and feasible by the Executive Engineer, Building Division. The executing Court directed the Receiver "to take up the construction works according to the approved estimates and supervision of the day to day construction work. By its order dated 5-11-74, the Receiver was directed to manage the affairs of the construction in accordance with the direction of the Court and without interference from any quarters including the Trustees. 

 11. The Executing Court by its order dated 11-12-74 rejected the application for stay of the work of the Receiver on the ground that the said application had been filed at a very belated state and that there was no reason to stay his work of the Receiver who had started the work long before. As against the said order, the application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been moved in this was on which Civil Rule No. 1365 of 1974 was issued on 17-12-74 and also an ad interim order was made staying the work of the Receiver till the disposal of the application for cancellation of the appointment of the Receiver had been make. 

 12. The application for cancellation of the appointment of the Receiver was heard on 1-1-75. The learned Subordinate Judge, by his order on the said date rejected the said application with the observation that the Receiver had already taken up the task for construction of a huge building involving good amount of money 'which had already been spent for the said construction and that such construction being in the greater interest and welfare of the beneficiaries decree-holders, suspension of the work would do great harm to them. As regards certain allegations as to abuse of power, the learned Subordinate Judge observed that appropriate steps might be taken for determining the liability and responsibility of the Receiver by appointing an Account Commissioner. Against the said order F.M.A.T. No. 21 of 1975 has been filed in this Court on 6-1-75 this Court by an order dated 8-1-75 directed that the appeal and the revision should be heard analogously. 

 14. The Rule issued in the Civil Revision, by its very term as well as that of the prayer made in the application for revision has become in fructuous, as the application for cancellation of the appointment of the Receiver pending the hearing of which the stay of the Receiver's work was prayed for has been heard and disposed of. On merits, the said Rule and absolutely no substance. Refusal to stay the construction works undertaken by the Receiver pending the filing of an application for removal of the Receiver can hardly be taken to be a case decided within the meaning of section I l5 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor there is any quest ion of jurisdiction, in the said order of the learned Subordinate Judge. The learned Subordinate Judge as perfectly within his powers to refuse to stay the Receiver's work in anticipation of an application which might be filed for cancellation of the Receiver's appointment. There was nothing before the Court from which the Court, could come to a conclusion that the Receiver's work was illegal or unauthorized and it cannot be said that the Court failed to exercise its jurisdiction in not preventing further progress of an illegal or unauthorized act. It was really a premature application, anticipating application challenging the validity of the appointment of the Receiver. 

 16. This appeal is directed against the order dated 1-1-75 purporting to reject, the application filed by the appellants on 29-11-74 for cancellation of the appointment of the Receiver. Respondent No. 1 was appointed as Receiver long back as on 3-9-73 i.e. more than 1 year and 2 months ago. The grounds taken in the Memorandum of Appeal as well as the contentions urged before us in this appeal merely relate to the validity or propriety of the order of appointment of the Receiver. No appeal was taken against the said order, although the order was appealable. This appeal cannot be taken to be an appeal against the aforesaid order of appointment of the Receiver, as such an appeal has long been barred by limitation, and no case for condonation of delay in filing the appeal has sought to be made out at any stage. Mr. M.H. Khondker, the learned Advocate for the appellant has, of course, contended that the order of appointment of Receiver having been made without jurisdiction was a nullity and as such it can be urged at any stage in order to bring the null order to the notice of the Court for necessary rectification. We shall deal with this contention of the learned Advocate at the appropriate place. We shall however have to decide whether the appeal against the older dated 1-1-75 as it stands, can be thrown away on the ground that no appeal lies against the said order purporting to refuse to cancel the order of appointment of the Receiver. Such a refusal may, of course, be construed as nothing else than a refusal to remove the Receiver. On the question of appeal ability of such an order, there appears to have been a conflict of judicial view. 

 17. The earliest case on this question appears to be that of Calcutta High Court, being the case of Shahebjada Faridun Shika Vs. Muhammad and others reported in 24 I.C. 802, in which Mukherjee and Neschareff JJ. were of the view that an order removing receiver was not an order under section 204 of the old Code of Civil Procedure (analogous to Order 40 Rule 1 C.P. Code) and as such was not appealable and in the case of Eastern Mortgage and Agency Co. Ltd. Vs. Premananda Saha and others reported in 20 C.W.N. 789 same case A.I.R. 1916 Calcutta 624 under the new code also it was held that no appeal lay from an order refusing to remove a receiver. This view of the Calcutta High Court appears to have been followed by the Madras High Court in the case of Ramaswarai Naidu and others Vs. Avvalu Naidu, reported in A.I.R. 1924 Madras 614 same case 78 Indian case 625. The Calcutta High Court, appears, however, to have shed new light on this question in the case of Sripati Dutta Vs. Bibhuti Bhusan Dutta, reported in A.I.R. 1926 Cal. 593, same case ILR 53 Cal. 319 same case 92 I.C. 940. where it has been laid down that an order dismissing an application for removal of a receiver may be construed to be an order under Order 40 rule 1 C.P. Code and as such it is appealable. It has been pointed out it the said case that when a person is authorized to do an act it is necessarily implied, according to section 16 of General Clauses Act that he is empowered to under the act and the power to appoint includes the power to remove or dismiss. The Court empowered to appoint a receiver under clause (a) of rule 1 of Order 40 of the Code, it has the necessary power to remove the receiver under the provision of the Code, read with section 16 of the General Clauses Act, and so an order of removal of receiver is necessarily an order under rule (1) of Order 40., and as such it is appealable under Order 43 rule 1(s) of the Code.  The Allahabad High Court however dissented from the above view of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Anthony Ullyssess John and others Vs. Agra United Mills Ltd. and another reported in A.I.R. 1931 Allahabad 72, same case 134 IC. 454. The High Court of Rangoon, however, has followed the later Calcutta view reported in A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta 593, in preference to that propounded in the earlier case reported in A T.R. 1916 Calcutta 824 in the case of Abdul Kader VS. R. M. P. Chattyar Film in A.I.R. 1938 Ran. 387 same case 178 I.C. 924 and held that an order refusing to remove a receiver is appealable. The Allahahad High Court appears to have revised its earlier view in the case of Allahabad Bank Ltd. Vs. Maharaj Kishore Khanna and others, in A.I.R. 1945 All 371 in which it dissented from the view expressed in A.I.R. 1931 All 72 and followed that of the Calcutta High Court, as expressed in A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta 593. The Patna High Court, in the case of Surendra Nath Sarkar Vs. Nagar Chand Goenka and another reported in A.I.R. 1947 Pat. 418 same case 25 Patna 779 made a distinction between an order removing a receiver and an order refusing to remove a receiver. Fazl Ali J (as he then was) in delivering the judgment the Court has held, following 20 C.W.N. 789, in A.I.R. 1924 Madras 614 and A.I.R. 1931 All 72, that although an order removing a receiver may be deemed to be an order under Rule 1 of Order 40, but an order refusing to remove a receiver cannot be deemed to be an order under the said provision, and as such it is not appealable. This judicial controversy was sought to be set at rest, so far as the courts in Indian jurisdiction were concerned, by the Federal Court of India in the case of Kutoor Vengayil Rayarappan Nayanar Vs. Rutoor Vengayil Valla Madhavi Amma and others, reported in A.I.R. 1950 F. C. 140, in which the view of the Calcutta High Court as expressed in A.I.R. 1926 'Calcutta 593 was approved and those expressed in A.I.R. 1916 Calcutta 824, 1924 a Mad. 614 and 1931 All 72 were disapproved. Mahajan J in delivering the judgment of the Federal Court observed as follows : 

 "It does not appear to have the appreciated that section 16 General Clauses Act, does not confer a new right on the Court to remove a receiver. It only furnishes a rule of interpretation and enacts that a power of appointment includes and implies within itself the poker of removal and wherever a Court is empowered to make a certain appointment automatically it gets authority to exercise the power of removal in respect of the person appointed." 

 The learned Judge in another part of the judgment after referring to the decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta 593 made the following observation: 

 The High Court of Travancore-Cochin in Indian jurisdiction without noticing the aforesaid Federal Court decision followed the view of the Patna High Court as expressed in A. I. R. 1947 Patna 418 in the case or Kochu Kumari Vs. Krishnan Janardhanan, Reported in, A.I.R. 1952 Travancore-Cochin 248 on the question of appeal ability of an order of refusal to remove receiver but the position was set right by the same High Court in a subsequent decision in the case of Velayudhan Narayanan Vs. Matheran Narayani and others, reported In A.I.R. 1955 Travancore-Cochin 163 in which the view expressed in A.I.R. 1950 (F. C.) 140 was followed. 

 18. We find ourselves in respectful agreement with the view expressed by the Federal Court of India in the above mentioned case and hold that the order under appeal pm ported to be an order refusing to remove the receiver was made under rule 1 of Order 40, and as such it cannot be said that the order is not appealable. 

 20. Mr. Khondker, the learned Advocate for the appellants, however, has tried to challenge in this appeal, the validity of the order of appointment of the Receiver, although no exception was taken to the said order within the period prescribed by law. The order was passed as long back as on 3.9.73 and in the interested parties stood by and apparent acquiesced in the said order. The Receiver appointed by the Court entered into his officio and proceeded to undertake various steps according to the direction of the Court in the discharge of the duties connected with his office. The order was appealable but no appeal having been preferred against the said order within the period of limitation the same has become final and the validity of the said order cannot be impugned indirectly in the appeal which has been preferred against a subsequent order. 

 21. Mr. Khondker has sought to buttress his stand in respect of his challenge against the order of appointment of the Receiver by submitting that the said order was in excess of the jurisdiction of the Court and vitas therefore a nullity and that a void order can be brought to the notice of the Court at any stage for its nullification. 

 22. Mr. S. A. Paul, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the added respondents has contended, relying upon the decision of the judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Ram Kirpal Shukul Vs. Mussamat Rup Murari, in 11 A.I.R. 37, that a judicial order which has not been set aside by a superior Court in an appropriate proceeding cannot be challenged at a subsequent stage, however defective or erroneous the said order may be, and has drawn our attention to the following passage of the judgment of the Court : 

 "It was said that a special appeal from that judgment did not lie to the High Court. If so, the judgment was final; if an appeal did lie and none was preferred the judgment was equally final and binding upon the parties and those claiming under them. It would be reproach upon the administration of justice if, after endeavoring for eleven years to obtain execution for mesne profits in accordance with a judgment of a Court of competent jurisdiction against which no appeal was preferred, the parties could now be told that judgment was erroneous, and that they were not entitled to mesne profits. 

 "It may of course, be contended that the said decision does not provide a complete answer to the contention raised by Mr. Khondker. It has laid down the law with regard to an order passed by an executing Court at an earlier stage that no challenge can be made against such an order at a subsequent stage. It is true that an order given by a competent Court is binding upon the parties to the proceeding in which the said order has been made however erroneous or defective the said order has been made, however erroneous or defective the said order may be, but such is not the case with an order which is made without jurisdiction. Such an order is a nullity and is non est in the eye of law and does not therefore stand in any need of being get aside. Mr. Khondker, the learned Advocate for the appellants has, therefore, tried to take recourse to the said principle and contained that the learned Subordinate Judge had no legal competence to make that order of appointment of the Receiver, which he purported to make and that as such they said was null and void an the learned Subordinate Judge could, in the said prentice, enquire into the said question at any subsequent stage of the proceeding and rectify his own mistake in having passed the said order, by recalling the same. In that event, of course, the learned Advocate has submitted, the impugned order may not be appealable, but as the learned Subordinate Judge failed to exercise his jurisdiction in not recalling the order which he made without jurisdiction, this court can treat the Memorandum of appeal as an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and grant necessary relief. 

 23. Mr. Khondker has attempted to develop his point by contending that the decree under execution is really one for specific performance of a contract and that the only way in which such a decree can be executed is by following the provisions as laid down in Oder 21, rule 34 C. P. C. The provisions of the Code being sufficient for execution of such a decree, resort to the assistance of a Receiver appointed by the Court for the purpose of execution is not contemplated under the law and as such the appointment was without any authority. The learned Advocate has submitted that though it is clear from Order 40 rule 1 of the Code that a Receiver can be appointed even after a decree has been passed but the only occasion for appointment of a Receiver after a decree has been passed is according to section, 51(d); C.P.C. Code, for the purpose of executing the decree. The learned Advocate has cited the case of Raja Birendra Nath Roy Bahadur Vs. Puran Chandra Nithatta, 67 C.L.J. 235, for the purpose of showing that the provisions of Order 21 rule 34 C. P. Code is available for the purpose of execution of the instant compromise decree and, as such, recourse to the provision of Order 40 of the Code for such execution was not according to law. The appointment of a receiver in an execution proceeding has the sanction of law, the learned Advocate has argued, only when the ordinary legal remedy of execution is not feasible. The learned Advocate has referred to the English principles for appointment of a Receiver and has invited our attention to the following passage from "Kerr on the Law and Practice as to Receivers", Thirteenth Edition (1963), at page 5. 

 "A receiver can only be properly appointed for the purpose of getting in and holding or securing funds or other property, which the Court at the trial or in the course of the action will have the means of distributing amongst or making over to the persons or person entitled thereto. The object sought by such appointment is therefore the safeguarding of property for the benefit of those entitled to it. There are two main classes of cases in which the appointment is made: (1) to enable persons who possess rights over property to obtain the benefit of those rights and to preserve the property pending realization, where ordinary legal remedies are defective and (2) to preserve property from some danger which threatens it." 

 24. The learned Advocate has also referred to certain decisions and has placed them before us, in support of his aforesaid contention. On an examination of the aforesaid authorities, it does not appear to us that there is any question of want of jurisdiction in the Court in making the order of appointment of the Receiver in the instant case. 

 25. In the first class of cases referred to in the passage quoted from Kerr on Receiver is included the cases in execution of decrees, which are known in English law, as equitable execution, i.e. where the appointment Is make to enable a judgment-creditor to obtain payment out of property which cannot be reached by legal execution. In the present case, according to the terms of the compromise decree, the decree holders were entitled to immediate possession and enjoyment of the properties in question, but it has been seen from the various proceedings taken during the course of the last several years that it has not been possible for the decree holders to get possession of the properties and reap the benefits of the decree by means of legal execution. It is precisely in an execution proceeding like this that the Court can, according to the English principle quoted above, exercise his power of appointment of a receiver. In this country of course, the entire law as to appointment of a receiver is contained in Order 40 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where the Court has been given wide powers of appointment of a receiver whenever if considers just and convenient to do so whether before or after the passing of the decree. 

 26. The observation of Chief Justice Rankin, of the Calcutta High Court, in the case of Pramatha Nath Malia Vs. H. V. Low & Co. in 34 C W.N. 238 may be referred to in this connection 

 "In England the appointment of a Receiver is often regarded as a form of equitable execution but in re. Sheppard (1889) 43 Ca. D. 131, the Court of Appeal pointed out that the expression tends to error. What a creditor gets by the appointment of a Receiver is not execution but a substitute for execution, a form of equitable relief which is granted on the ground that there is no effective remedy by execution at law. Accordingly there is authority for the proposition that a person seeking "equitable execution" must show that he was met by difficulties arising from the nature of property which prevent, his obtaining relief at law. In India the distinction between legal and equitable interest is not observed in the full sense in which it is part of the law in England. Since 1908, at all events, provision has been made by the Code for the appointment of a Receiver as a form of execution." 

 27. In another case cited from the same volume being the case of Dhirendra Krishna Deb and others Vs. Surendra Krishna Nandi and others, reported in 34 C.W.N. 440, it has been explained what is the true import of the expression" "just and convenient" and it has been pointed out that it does not mean that the Court is to appoint a receiver only because the Court thinks it convenient, but it means that the Court could male an appointment for proteci on of the rights or prevention of injury according to legal principles. 

 28. The Privy Council decision in the case of Sir Wasif Ali Minza, Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad Vs. The Karmani Industrial Bank Ltd., in 35 C.W.N. 791, as referred to by the learned Advocate for the appellants, does not lay down any new principle, but barely recognises that by section 51, the Court is empowered on the application of a decree-holder to order execution of the decree, inter alia (d) by appointing a receiver. Relying upon this decision, Mr. Khondker has sought to argue that the appointment of a receiver in an execution proceeding was nothing but a mode of execution, and that the decree under execution being one for execution and registration of deeds of transfer, the sole object of appointment of a receiver could be execution and registration of the said deeds and that appointment of a receiver for any other purpose was beyond the purview of Order 40 read with Section 51(d) of the Code. 

 29. It will be pertinent to mention in this connection two other cases of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, viz. the cases of Lal Rejandra Narayan Singh Vs. Mr. Sunder Bibi, L. R. 52 I.A. 262, same case, 30 C.W.N. 818, same case A.I.R. 1925 P.C. 176, and Ma Mya and another Vs. Ma Me Kyin and another, in 34 C.W.N. 117 (P. C.), where appointment of receiver was held by the Judicial Committee to be approve in execution of money decrees. Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad's case (35 C.W.N. 791) and Las Rajendra Narayan's case 30 C.W.N. 819) arose out of the proceedings in execution of money decrees, and Ma Mya's arose out of a suit for a declaration of plaintiffs title to half share of the family properties. In the former two cases, the properties proceeded against in execution proceedings were in possession of the judgment-debtors in limited right for their maintenance and as such appointment of a receiver was considered to be appropriate remedies. In the third case (34 C.W.N. 117, which arose out of a suit, the Judicial Committee affirmed the finding of the High Court declaring one third share of the Respondents in the assets of the family, mostly consisting of promissory notes and observed that the right method of working out the decree in such a case was by appointment of a receiver to realize the Monies due on the notes and pay over to the Respondents the third shares of the recoveries to which they had been held entitled. 

 30. On a consideration of these cases, it is clear that there is no warrant for the position taken by the learned Advocate for the Appellants that a Receiver may be appointed in an execution proceeding only for carrying out the specific direction in the decree. Section 51(d) of the Code no doubt provides for appointment of a Receiver as one of the several modes of execution of a decree, but it also indicates that such power can be exercised only in accordance with the rules referred to in section 121 of the Code, and Order 40 incorporates the relevant rules. The predominant condition therefore, for the exercise of such a power, is that in the opinion of the Court concerned such a measure should be just and convenient. 

 "The Codes of 1877 and 1882 gave a general power for the appointment of a receiver. Under the Code of 1908, appointment of a receiver as a mode of execution was recognized by section 51 and the words of Or: 40 rule 1 were altered to enlarge the powers of the Court by providing that the Court may appoint receivers not only in suits but in all proceedings, including proceedings in execution of decrees and in every case in which it appears to the court just and convenient to do so. As regards the circumstances which would justify such appointment, cases under the old code are not altogether negligible, because they lay down principles which are sound principles of equity and so are generally the principles of universal application. 

 32. It is to be noticed that in the above-mentioned case, the order of appointment of a receiver in respect of a defaulting tenure in 4 Rent Execution cases for realization of the decrees for rents was set aside by the High Court on the ground that ordinary remedy of execution was available to the decree-holder and no special equities could be shown in favor of the Parties concerned. The view of the learned Judges were expressed in the following words: 

 "Much more care should be taken ascertain whether the order should be made in a case where the decree holder having the ordinary remedy of execution available to him applies for the appointment of a receiver to pay himself out in respect of his decree, keeping the property fixed upon the judgment-debtor with all his liabilities intact in respect thereof and yet depriving him of its enjoyment and its profits. It should be noted that one of the several positions taken by the judgments-debtors in this case in the Court below in opposing the appointment of a receiver was that there was no reason why the decree-holders should not realize their dues by the ordinary process of putting up the properties for sale. The order which the learned Judge has made under section 51 C.P.C. in the case before us, has been made almost as a matter of course and far from satisfying the requirements of the phrase" just and convenient" occurring in order 40 Rule 1 C.P.C. which must necessarily mean just and convenient in view of the equities in favor of both the parties is, in our opinion, exactly the reverse, so far as the judgment-debtors are concerned." 

 "In one sense, no doubt, the suit in the present case has not come to an end but whether the appointment is regarded as made in the suit or in execution, what the Court has to see is whether the appointment appears to the Court to be just and convenient within the meaning of Order 40 and Rule 1 of the Code. It is obvious that whets the question arises, after a mortgage decree for sale, whether a receiver should be appointed in respect of the properties to be sold, in order to see whether it would be just and convenient to make the appointment, one must consider what impediment there is or there may be for sale to be held." 

 34. Mr. Khondker has also cited the case of Thacker's Press and Directories Ltd Vs. Metropolitan Bank Ltd. and another decided by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court reported in 67 C. W. N. 350 in support of his contention that where there is a Specific provision like order 21, Rule 34 C.P.C. for execution of the decree, there cannot be an appointment of a receiver under Section 51(d) of the Code, but strictly speaking, the said case does not appear, in our opinion, relevant for our present consideration as, although elaborate arguments where advanced in the said case on the question of appointment of a receiver under section 51(d) of the Code, the impugned Order has been held to have been passed in that case under section 51(b) of the Code. The learned Judges have, made the following comment in dealing with the arguments at the bar, which may be of some interest for our purpose: 

 "Appointing a receiver is one of the modes of execution section 51 prescribes, so it is as much a legal mode as any other. An executing Court, considering whether or not appointment of a receiver is called for, will doubtless have Order 40, Rule 1 of the Code in mind and make the appointment only when it considers just and convenient to do so. To that extent it involves exercise of judicial discretion on equitable principles but thereby it does not cease to be a legal mode. The execution or the mode of execution is legal and statutory, that is, as prescribed in the Code, although, to the extent, the code does not prescribe any details and loaves the matter to be worked out by the Court, equitable exercise of the jurisdiction or judicial discretion is called for and contemplated." 

 36. Mr. S. R. Paul, the learned Advocate appearing for Added respondents and Mr. Moinul Hossain, the learned Advocate for respondents No. 1, the Receiver, has placed before us a number of decisions in support of their contentions that a Court has jurisdiction to appoint a receiver in an execution proceeding if it appears to be just sad convenient to the Court. Mention may be made, out of the cases, to the cases of Atta Ullah Khan Vs. Bala Mal A.I.R. 1927 Lahore 190, Mohammad Ishaq Vs. Om Prakash and others A.I.R. 1933 All. 227, Maran Mar Masselious Gheevarghese Vs. Most Rev. Paulose Mar Athanasius and another, in A.I.R. 1952 T. C. 308, S. Mar. Ramaswami Chattiar Vs. S M. A. M. RM. Ramaswami Chettiar, in A.I.R. 1964 Madras 39 and Bhagawatin and Vs. Ramchandra Pratap and another, A.I.R. 1964 Madhya Pradesh, 211. 

 "Even on the assumption that the suit had ended, it is difficult to uphold the contention that under Order XL rule 1, the Sub-ordinate Judge had no power, except in execution, to appoint a receiver. The rule expressly states that where it appears to the Court to be just and convenient "whether before or after decree". Shammugani Vs. Moidin, I.L.R. 8 Mad. 229 which was decided before the insertion in Order XL rule 1 of the words "whether before or after the decree" held that it was competent for the court to appoint a receiver even after a decree had been passed, otherwise than in execution. It was pointed out in that case that there was nothing in section 503 of the code as it then stood which restricted the court's power to appoint receiver after a suit had come to an end. It was evidently in view of this decision to make the matter beyond doubt the words "whether before or after decree" were inserted." 

 38. A similar view has been expressed in the case reported in A.1.R. 1964 M. P. 211 in which the decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Hementha Nath Vs. Prakash Chandra, 35 C.W.N. 1066 has been distinguished, and the learned Single Judge after quoting a passage from the aforesaid Calcutta case, which has already been reproduced by us at page 42 of this judgment, has made the following observation : 

 "I think, with great respect, no exception can possible be taken to the proposition as such in the abstract but I am unable to regard it as an inflexible rule that whenever there is no impediment to execution and that remedy is available to the plaintiff, he can never ask for a receiver. Circumstances and facts may well exist which may properly lead the Court to a conclusion that it will be just and convenient to appoint a receiver, notwithstanding the fact that the plaintiff had a remedy by way of execution. The application of the proposition laid down in the Calcutta case will depend upon the facts and circumstances in each case. 

 A close examination of all the relevant judicial authorities does not leave any doubt in any One's mind that there cannot be any question as to the jurisdiction of an executing Court to pass an order of appointment of a Receiver, whatever may be the stage of execution. There may be a scope for difference of opinion as to the propriety of an order of appointment of a receiver, depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case, but there appears to be absolutely no basis, statutory or otherwise for the argument that the order of appointment of the Receiver was without jurisdiction. 

 "51. Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, the Court may, on the application of the decree-holder, order execution of the decree 

 Section 94 In order to prevent the ends of justice from being defeated, the court may, if it is so prescribed, 

 (1) Where it appears to the Court to be just and convenient the Court may by order, 

 (d) confer upon the. receiver all such powers, as to bring; he, and defending suits and for the realization, management, protection, preservation and improvement of the property, the collection of the rents and profits thereof, the application and disposal of such rents and profits, and the execution of documents as the owner himself has, or suet, of those powers as the Court thinks fit. 

 (2) Nothing in this rule shall authorize the Court to remove from the possession of custody of property any person whom any party to the suit has not a present 'right so to remove." 

 40. The powers which have been conferred upon a Court by section 51 including the making of an order directing execution of a decree by appointment of a Receiver is to be exercised "subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed." 

 Sec. 94 also similarly empowers a Court to make various kinds of order including an order appointing a receiver in order to prevent the ends of justice from being defeated "if it is so prescribed". 

 41. The conditions and limitations as have been contemplated in the aforesaid two provisions have been prescribed in the various rule of Order 40 of the Code. The dominant objective for making use of the said powers of Making appointment of a Receiver under the said provisions is, of course, prevention of the cause of justice which a person seeks to establish in legal proceeding from being defeated and also execution of a decree which a person may have obtained in a suit. The scope of section 94 does not appear to be confined to a suit only and it may be invoked in an execution proceeding as well. But the power under section 51 can he exercised only for the purpose of execution of a decree. From the language used in rule (1) of Order 40 also it is clear that the authority to appoint a Receiver does not end with the passing of a decree and the Court retains the power to appoint a receiver even after the passing of the decree and the only limitation which has been impose under the said rule is that the measure should appear to be just and convenient to the Court. What is just and convenient does certainly depend upon the facts and circumstances in each case. The various decisions which have been referred to above also make it clear that the provision of section 51 (d) does not provide for the only circumstances in which a Receiver can be appointed after the passing of a decree. The said provision provides, no doubt, that one of the modes of execution of a decree is by appointment of a Receiver but a Receiver can also be appointed in an execution proceeding for a purpose other than immediate execution of the decree if such an appointment is in consonance with the principle of justice and convenience of the parties e.g. for the preservation and protection of a judgment-debtor's property pending execution of the decree so that the purpose of the decree may not be frustrated. The power of the Court in appointing a Receiver in an execution proceeding cannot be circumscribed by the objective referred to in section 51(d) only. On the other hand, in a case where there is impediment to the execution of a decree in an ordinary course and there are special equities in favor of the parties to the proceeding, a Receiver may be appointed in an execution proceeding, an in order to confer the benefits of the decree upon the decree-holder, who is rightfully entitled to the same. Such an appointment will fulfill the objective of section 51(d) of the Code. 

 42. The Legislature has made provisions in clause (a) of rule 1 of Order 40 of the Code for appointment of a Receiver whether before or after the decree, and in clause (c) of the said rule for committing a property to the possession custody or management of the Receiver Powers can be conferred upon him under clause (d) of the rule for management, protection, preservation and improvement of the property, the collection of the rents and profits thereof the application and disposal of such rents and profits, and the execution of documents as the owner himself has. It does not appear that the said powers can be made available only in a case when the order of appointment has been made in a pending suit before the passing of the decree. From a perusal of the provisions referred to above it is clear to us that the powers mentioned in clause (d) of S. 51 are available to a Court also in execution stage also in an appropriate case and such powers can be exercised for the purpose of management, protection, preservation and improvement of a property if it appears to the Court that it will advance the cause of justice and will be of ultimate benefit to the parties concerned. 

 43. If we examined the facts of the instant case in the light of the legal provisions referred to above, we find that in this case the decree holders had taken all available steps under the law for execution of the compromise decree winch has been obtained in ore year 1959. The present execution case has been started in 1963. The part of the decree relating to payment of money has already been executed, but the part relating to execution and registration of deeds of transfer in respect of certain properties and delivery of vacant possession thereof, directed in the terms of the compromise has not yet been executed. As a matter of fact, draft kabala as contemplated in Order 21 rule 34 C P Code has been filed as back as in 1964. But in spite of the best efforts it has been not been possible for the Court to execute and register the necessary deed, although the judgment-debtors in this case appear to be cooperative with the decree holders for the execution of the necessary deeds. As has been stated above, because of the fact that the judgment debtors are numerous in number and are living in different parts of the world, it has not been possible to obtain the Income Tax Clearance Certificate but for which the necessary deeds cannot be executed and registered. It is a very peculiar case in which the judgment-debtors are not inclined to offer any resistance to the prayer of the decree holder for execution of the decree or for appointment of a receiver. On the contrary, the judgment-debtors themselves have submitted to the Court that because of non-execution of the deeds of transfer and failure of the decree-holders to take possession of the property in question, the judgment-debtors have been suffering heavy loss. It is the case where, as it appears to us, the interests of the decree-holders and the judgment-debtors in the matter of taking possession of the property or management of the same by a Receiver are identical. It does therefore appear to be rather intriguing to find that some persons describing themselves as decree-holders or beneficiaries have chosen to oppose the decree-holders prayer for appointment of a Receiver. This opposition is calculated to serve the purpose of neither party and seeks to deprive the decree-holders of the benefits of the decree with no corresponding gain to the judgment-debtors. 

 44. The appointment of the Receiver as has been made in the present case is by way of execution of the decree by which vacant possession of the land has been directed to be made over to the decree-holders on execution and registration of the requisite deeds of transfer. The history of the case has made it abundantly clear that there are great impediments to the execution of the decree in the ordinary way causing loss to both the judgment-debtor as well as the decree-holders and it is precise in a case like this that equitable execution by appointment of a n receiver has been prescribed. The appointment of the Receiver in this case, is justified also on the ground of protection, preservation and improvement of the properties to which the decree-holders right has been established by the terms of the said decree. There is no doubt as to the legal title of the decree holders to get possession of the property, as it has been clearly provided in the compromise decree that the judgment debtors shall transfer the property and also deliver vacant possession of the same to the decree-holders and more than 12 years have since passed. In our opinion, having regard to the facts of the case the executing. Court was perfectly within his power to appoint the Receiver for the purpose of executing the decree, as well as for protecting and preserving the property for the benefits of the persons in whose favour the decree has been made. In the circumstances of the case it cannot therefore be said that the executing court acted beyond its jurisdiction in appointing receiver. 

 45. We therefore, hold that even if the appeal is taken to be an application for revision under section 115 C.P.C. as against the order purporting to be one of refusal of the executing court to recall an order, alleged to have been passed without jurisdiction, we do not find any substance in the same. 

 47. After delivery of the judgment Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants prays for a stay of the operation of the order made by us till the appellants obtain an order of stay from Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. Having regard to the facts of the case we do not think that the appellant will be very much prejudiced if the order of stay is not granted.
